newsitem.title: UK: Enterprise impresses with low finding costs.
newsitem.headline: Enterprise impresses with low finding costs.

text.p: Enterprise Oil's profits may have come in at the low end of market expectations, but analysts still found plenty of evidence that the exploration and production company faces a bright future.

Higher dividends and a higher production forecast all helped to instill more confidence, but the figure that pleased most was the low average finding cost of 99 pence per barrel of oil equivalent, analysts said.
Together with reserve additions of 160 millions barrels and a production replacement of 193 percent, Enterprise last year laid the foundations for solid profit growth in coming years.
"You've got a high level of reserve replacement at a very cost effective level. It basically means you're building in long-term profitable growth in the business," said Colin Smith at BZW.
Enterprise already started to show last year it was on the right track as finds in Italy helped it regain investors' confidence, which it had lost after its failed bid for LASMO Plc in 1994.
"What you're after are E&P companies than can renew themselves at a reasonable cost and that's what Enterprise is doing," said an analyst at a leading broker.

He added there was no reason to be disappointment about Enterprise's 1996 profit which was only lower than many industry watchers had forecast simply because the company used a good year to make bigger exploration write-offs than necessary.
Enterprise's profit after tax rose 40 percent to 142.5 million stg, while analysts had expected a figure nearer to 151 million.
While analysts gave their thumbs up to Enterprise, none was convinced the results would add much extra fuel to the company's shares which were the FTSE 100's best performers last year.
"Enterprise is a very good company, but it's pretty much up with events," said BZW's Smith.
